checkpoints: A default `etcd3` read is linearizable, meaning it triggers a ReadIndex confirmation: before answering, the leader verifies via a majority heartbeat that it is still leader. No log entry is written, but the client still pays roughly one leader round-trip per read.

Calling `.serializable()` on an `etcd3` `GetBuilder` skips the ReadIndex confirmation entirely and answers straight from whichever replica received the request. This is nearly free but can lag the true committed state by tens of milliseconds — a bounded staleness, not an unbounded one.

Reads split into two categories by what they're used for: reads that DECIDE something (who holds a lock, who is leader, critical config) versus reads that only DISPLAY something (a dashboard count, a metrics aggregate). This distinction, not raw call frequency, determines which consistency mode a read needs.

A stale answer on a lock-owner or leadership read can hand the same lock or leadership role to two different callers at once, so that read must stay linearizable — it cannot be switched to `.serializable()`.

A dashboard or metrics read that is off by tens of milliseconds causes no correctness problem, only a slightly stale display value, so it is safe to switch to `.serializable()` and read from the local replica instead of paying the round-trip on every poll.

The fix is a per-call routing decision, not a global consistency downgrade: only the reads that tolerate staleness get `.serializable()` added; reads that gate a decision are left on the default linearizable path untouched.

The win can be proven by measuring p99 latency under load for both paths — the switched-over dashboard read should drop close to a local read, while the lock-owner read stays at roughly one round-trip, unchanged.

The routing rule itself should be enforced by a test, not just documented: spy on the underlying `get(...).exec()` call for the lock-owner read and assert that `.serializable()` is never chained onto it, so a future edit can't silently weaken a decision-making read.
